artboards.title: 5 · Verdict — each direction owns a band

annotations.text:
FIVE BLENDS OF THE SAME THREE DIRECTIONS.

The three sources differ on axes that do not overlap, which is what makes blending possible at all:

  Instrument  the GRID — hairline columns, mono micro-labels, tabular figures, em dash for absent.
  Editorial   the VOICE — Instrument Serif, and one figure per screen allowed to be large.
  Depth       the MATERIAL — recessed and raised planes, one light source, glow only for live status.

Each blend below changes WHICH AXIS LEADS. That is the real decision — not the colour, which is already shared.

  1 Composed   No leader. Depth is the chrome, Instrument the working grid, Editorial the title and one hero.
  2 Briefing   Editorial leads. The screen tells you something in a sentence before it shows a number. No cards at all; Depth is almost absent because material would fight the type.
  3 Terminal   Instrument leads, hard. Zero radius, hairlines, mono everywhere, twelve figures visible at once. Editorial gets exactly one word. For an owner who lives on this screen.
  4 Panels     Depth leads. Four big lit panels instead of twelve tiles; material does the grouping that borders used to. The warning panel is its own lit surface.
  5 Verdict    Nothing blends — each direction owns a BAND. Editorial floats on top with the answer; Instrument sits recessed beneath it with the evidence. Depth is the seam that makes them read as different kinds of thing.

All five share one type system: Archivo, IBM Plex Mono, Instrument Serif. Figtree and JetBrains Mono are dropped — six families is how a blend dies.

Every board carries the new rail: a context switch instead of the invented "Mine" group, and "Plans & payments" instead of "Money". Both are already live in the code.

The three originals, kept for comparison. Same Overview screen, same content, same palette in each — so what you are reading is the direction and not the data. Their rails still show the old "MINE" group, which is what started all of this.
